# Perturbation Recipes

Each recipe below is one or more entries for the `conditions:` list in
`config/ChromSimConfig.yaml`, with what it models, what to expect, and what to
watch out for. Every recipe works with the current pipeline: nothing to install
or code. The numbers are examples of the pattern, not recommendations: run a
small range and see which value matches your data.

All recipes follow the rules from the [vignette](vignette.qmd#adding-a-condition-to-test-a-hypothesis):
change **one** setting relative to a condition you already have, give each
entry a new `name` and `params_name`, and count the cost: every condition adds
`n_replicates × n_shards` GPU jobs per locus (6 with the shipped settings).

## How the settings relate

The cohesin settings are not independent. Three relations explain most of
what the recipes do:

| Quantity | Formula | Shipped value |
|----------|---------|---------------|
| DNA extruded per cohesin leg before it falls off (processivity) | `lifetime × vlef` monomers | 75,000 × 0.0025 ≈ 190 kb |
| Number of cohesins on the chain | chain monomers / `separation` | one per 240 kb |
| Loop coverage: how much of the chain is inside a loop at once | about 2 × processivity / `separation` | ≈ 1.6 |

So doubling `lifetime` doubles how far each cohesin gets; halving `vlef` with
the same `lifetime` halves it; doubling `separation` halves the number of
cohesins. One monomer is `resolution` bp (1 kb by default).

All recipes below start from this baseline (the shipped `cond1_baseline`):

```yaml
  - name:         cond1_baseline
    params_name:  baseline
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

## Cohesin stays longer (WAPL loss)

**Models:** loss of WAPL, which releases cohesin from DNA, so cohesin stays
bound and extrudes further.

```yaml
  - name:         wapl-loss_2x
    params_name:  wapl_2x
    lifetime:     150000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1

  - name:         wapl-loss_5x
    params_name:  wapl_5x
    lifetime:     375000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** longer loops, reaching convergent CTCF pairs further apart, and
stronger stripes, as reported in WAPL-depleted Hi-C.

**Watch out:** a longer `lifetime` also needs longer equilibration; polysim
extends its warm-up to at least one cohesin lifetime automatically, so these
jobs take longer.

## Fewer cohesins (NIPBL or RAD21 depletion)

**Models:** partial loss of cohesin loading (NIPBL) or of cohesin itself
(RAD21 knockdown). Halving the amount of cohesin doubles `separation`.

```yaml
  - name:         cohesin-50pct
    params_name:  cohesin_50
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   480
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** weaker loops and domains everywhere, with the same positions.

**Watch out:** for complete cohesin loss, use `separation: none` (see
[No cohesin at all](#no-cohesin-at-all)).

## Weaker CTCF stalling (partial CTCF depletion)

**Models:** less CTCF bound at every site (a partial knockdown, or a mutant
that holds cohesin less well), without data on which sites are lost.

```yaml
  - name:         ctcf-weak_0.25
    params_name:  ctcf_025
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.25
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** weaker dots and boundaries, and more cohesin reading through
sites to the next convergent pair.

**Watch out:** this weakens every site equally. If you have CTCF data from the
perturbed cells, the next recipe is more faithful.

## CTCF degradation, with data

**Models:** a CTCF degron (auxin or dTAG) or any treatment where you profiled
CTCF. The sites themselves come from the perturbed sample.

Add the perturbed sample to the samplesheet (its Hi-C is optional):

```
Project  Cell_Type  Condition    CTCF_Peaks                              Hi-C
MyProj   mESC       untreated    /proj/yourlab/ctcf/untreated.narrowPeak    /proj/yourlab/hic/untreated.mcool
MyProj   mESC       ctcf_degron  /proj/yourlab/ctcf/auxin_6h.narrowPeak     /proj/yourlab/hic/auxin_6h.mcool
```

Then one condition per sample, identical except for the CTCF they use:

```yaml
  - name:         untreated
    params_name:  untreated
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    untreated
    compare_hic:  untreated

  - name:         ctcf-degron
    params_name:  degron
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    ctcf_degron
    compare_hic:  ctcf_degron
```

**Expect:** loops lost where the degron removes CTCF from an anchor; this is
the same design as the sorbitol `cond2_ctcf-only` condition.

**Watch out:** names, paths and assemblies must agree; run
`bash check_inputs.sh` after adding the samples.

## Stalled cohesin lives longer (or not)

**Models:** how much CTCF stabilizes cohesin once both legs are stalled
(`life_boost_stalled`, default 4 from the `polysim:` block). `1` means no
stabilization.

```yaml
  - name:         no-stall-boost
    params_name:  boost_1
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    life_boost_stalled: 1
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** with `1`, weaker dots at convergent pairs, since loops there come
apart as fast as anywhere else; with larger values, stronger dots.

## Slower extrusion

**Models:** cohesin stepping more slowly, e.g. under reduced ATP, or a
mutant motor.

```yaml
  - name:         slow-extrusion
    params_name:  slow
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    vlef:         0.00125
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** with the same `lifetime`, half the processivity (≈ 95 kb per
leg), so shorter loops and fewer distant dots.

**Watch out:** `vlef` and `lifetime` trade off (processivity is their
product). To change speed but not loop size, change both: `vlef: 0.00125`
with `lifetime: 150000`.

## No cohesin at all

**Models:** complete cohesin loss (e.g. RAD21 degradation). The chain is
simulated as a polymer with no loop extrusion; `lifetime` and the CTCF sites
are ignored.

```yaml
  - name:         no-cohesin
    params_name:  no_cohesin
    separation:   none
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** loops, stripes and domains disappear, and contacts fall off
smoothly with distance. Whatever remains is what the polymer does without
extrusion, which makes this the control for asking whether a feature needs
cohesin at all (see [sticky sites](#other-factors-sticky-sites)).

## CTCF strength from peak signal

**Models:** CTCF sites that differ in occupancy. Instead of one stall
probability for every site, each site's probability follows its CUT&Tag peak
signal: the weakest site in the locus gets `min`, the strongest `max`, and the
rest are spread evenly between them by rank.

```yaml
  - name:         ctcf-by-signal
    params_name:  ctcf_signal
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: {min: 0.2, max: 0.9}
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** fewer, more realistic dots: weak sites become leaky, so the
simulation stops drawing a strong dot at every convergent pair.

**Watch out:** the signal is the narrowPeak `signalValue` (column 7) of the
peak each site came from. Ranks are used, not raw values, so the peak
caller's scale doesn't matter, but the result does depend on `min` and `max`.

## Other factors: sticky sites

**Models:** factors that hold distant DNA together without extrusion:
dimerising bridges (YY1, LDB1), condensates (e.g. YAP under hyperosmotic
stress), enhancer–promoter contacts. The beads under a factor's peaks attract
each other in 3D, with an energy in kT; there is no orientation rule, and no
cohesin is needed.

Each factor's peaks come from a **new samplesheet column**, read from the row
of the condition's `ctcf_type` sample (or the one named by `sample:`):

```
Project  Cell_Type  Condition  CTCF_Peaks                       Hi-C                         YY1_Peaks                       LDB1_Peaks
MyProj   K562       control    /proj/yourlab/ctcf/ctl.narrowPeak  /proj/yourlab/hic/ctl.mcool    /proj/yourlab/yy1/ctl.narrowPeak  /proj/yourlab/ldb1/ctl.narrowPeak
```

One factor (YY1), with its like-for-like control:

```yaml
  - name:         yy1-control
    params_name:  yy1_ctl
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    attraction_energy: 0
    ctcf_type:    control
    compare_hic:  control

  - name:         yy1-sticky
    params_name:  yy1_2kT
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    sticky:
      - {factor: YY1, peaks: YY1_Peaks, energy: 2.0}
    ctcf_type:    control
    compare_hic:  control
```

Two factors, with an attraction between them too:

```yaml
  - name:         yy1-ldb1-sticky
    params_name:  yy1_ldb1
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    sticky:
      - {factor: YY1,  peaks: YY1_Peaks,  energy: 1.5}
      - {factor: LDB1, peaks: LDB1_Peaks, energy: 2.5}
    sticky_cross:
      - {factors: [YY1, LDB1], energy: 1.0}
    ctcf_type:    control
    compare_hic:  control
```

Options for each `sticky` entry: `factor` (a name), `peaks` (the samplesheet
column), `energy` (kT between two of its sites), `sample` (another sample's
row), `span` (`summit`, the default: the bead at each summit; or `peak`: every
bead the peak covers). A bead under several factors' peaks attracts each of
them with the strongest energy that applies.

**Expect:** dots between sticky sites in any orientation, including between
sites with no CTCF; with many sites, a checkerboard of contacts among them.
To test whether a loop is a bridge rather than extrusion, add the same
`sticky` to a `separation: none` condition: a bridge loop survives without
cohesin, an extrusion loop doesn't.

**Watch out:**

- **Use the control above** (`attraction_energy: 0`). Sticky beads switch
  polysim to its attraction-capable polymer force, whose repulsion has a
  slightly different shape from the default; a control that sets
  `attraction_energy` uses the same force, so the comparison is like for
  like.
- **The energy is unknown;** run a range (e.g. 1, 2, 3 kT). polysim's own
  enhancer–promoter example uses 3 kT. Too strong, and the sticky beads
  collapse into one cluster.
- **Peaks are a population average,** so a peak-based model overstates
  co-binding in any one cell.
- **For a factor without a DNA-binding domain** (LDB1 is recruited by GATA1,
  TAL1 or LHX proteins), use the factor's own ChIP or CUT&Tag if you have it:
  partner peaks overcount.

## Chromatin compaction

**Models:** chromatin as a whole becoming stickier or more compact, e.g.
under hyperosmotic stress. Every bead attracts every other bead weakly.

```yaml
  - name:         compact-0.1
    params_name:  compact_01
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    attraction_energy: 0.1
    ctcf_type:    condition2
    compare_hic:  condition2
```

**Expect:** more long-range contacts overall, so contact frequency falls
off more slowly with distance.

**Watch out:** compare against a condition with `attraction_energy: 0` (the
same polymer force; see the sticky-site control). Small values matter: start
around 0.05–0.2 kT.

## Where cohesin loads

**Models:** cohesin loading concentrated at some sites (e.g. NIPBL peaks,
active enhancers) instead of uniformly. Loading at the peaks is `boost` times
the background rate.

```yaml
  - name:         loading-at-enhancers
    params_name:  load_enh
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    loading:      {peaks: H3K27ac_Peaks, boost: 10}
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** stripes starting at loading sites, even where there is no CTCF.

**Watch out:** the total number of cohesins is unchanged (`separation`); only
where they land changes. polysim never loads cohesin at strong CTCF sites
(stall probability above 0.9).

## Where cohesin slows down

**Models:** obstacles to extrusion, e.g. RNA Pol II in transcribed genes.
At the peaks, cohesin legs step `slowdown` times less often.

```yaml
  - name:         pausing-at-polII
    params_name:  pause_pol2
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    pausing:      {peaks: PolII_Peaks, slowdown: 4, span: peak}
    ctcf_type:    condition1
    compare_hic:  condition1
```

**Expect:** weaker or fuzzier boundaries at transcribed regions, and loops
shifted along them. `span: peak` slows cohesin across each whole peak, which
suits broad gene-body signal.

## Calibrating to live imaging

**Models:** nothing new; it converts simulation units (monomers, frames) into
nm and seconds, so simulated loop lifetimes and distances can be compared with
imaging. This follows the polysim tutorial: simulate a chain **without
cohesin**, and match its two-point MSD to an imaging MSD from
cohesin-depleted cells (e.g. the Fbn2 ΔRAD21 data of Gabriele et al. 2022);
every other condition then reuses those units.

```yaml
conditions:
  - name:         no-cohesin
    params_name:  no_cohesin
    separation:   none
    ctcf_type:    condition1
  # ... your other conditions ...

analysis:
  msd: True
  calibration:
    default_anchor: msd
    msd:
      expt_msd:            {no-cohesin: /proj/yourlab/imaging/fbn2_dRAD21_msd.csv}
      reference_condition: no-cohesin
```

The CSV has two columns, `dt_s` and `msd_um2`: lag time in seconds and MSD
in µm². The no-cohesin condition is calibrated against it; every other
condition waits for it and writes the same nm/monomer and s/frame into its
`*_calibration.json`.

**Watch out:** the imaging probes should sit about as far apart as the
simulated MSD probe pairs (`analysis.msd_probe`). `msd: True` makes the
analysis much slower.

## A 1D screen before 3D runs

Every 3D condition costs GPU time. The 1D engine alone (cohesin moving on the
CTCF track, no polymer) runs in seconds to minutes on a CPU, and tells you,
for each setting, how often each convergent CTCF pair is held by a cohesin
(its **looped fraction**), the mean loop size, and how much of the chain is
inside loops:

```bash
bash sweep_1d.sh --condition cond1_baseline --lifetime 37500,75000,150000 --ctcf-capture 0.25,0.5 --out sweep_1d.tsv
```

Every combination of the comma-separated values is run (6 here); any
setting not given keeps the condition's value (`--separation`, `--vlef`,
`--life-boost-stalled` work the same way). `--loops` scores the loops in a
TSV (columns `chrom`, `anchor1`, `anchor2`) instead of every convergent pair.
It needs the oriented CTCF files of a run (`sbatch ChromSimPipe.sh --until
validateCTCF`), and loading and pausing options apply; sticky sites act in
3D only and are ignored. Run larger sweeps on a compute node.

**Use it to:** pick a sensible range before a 3D robustness run, or check
that a perturbation changes the loops you care about at all.

## A robustness range

Before trusting a conclusion, check it holds over a few cohesin settings,
for every condition you compare. For example, three lifetimes for the
control–treated pair from the sorbitol example (6 conditions):

```yaml
  - {name: ctl_life-0.5x, params_name: ctl_l05, lifetime: 37500,  separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition1, compare_hic: condition1}
  - {name: ctl_life-1x,   params_name: ctl_l1,  lifetime: 75000,  separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition1, compare_hic: condition1}
  - {name: ctl_life-2x,   params_name: ctl_l2,  lifetime: 150000, separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition1, compare_hic: condition1}
  - {name: trt_life-0.5x, params_name: trt_l05, lifetime: 37500,  separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition2, compare_hic: condition2}
  - {name: trt_life-1x,   params_name: trt_l1,  lifetime: 75000,  separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition2, compare_hic: condition2}
  - {name: trt_life-2x,   params_name: trt_l2,  lifetime: 150000, separation: 240, ctcf_capture: 0.5, ctcf_type: condition2, compare_hic: condition2}
```

This is YAML's one-line form of the same entries: each `{...}` is one
condition. If the control-vs-treated conclusion (e.g. "CTCF explains the lost
loops") holds at all three lifetimes, it doesn't depend on that choice.

## Simulating without Hi-C

A sample with CTCF peaks but no Hi-C (`NA` in the samplesheet) can still be
simulated: leave `compare_hic` out of its condition. You get the simulated
maps, P(s), insulation and APA, without the comparison metrics. This is how to
make a prediction for a condition you haven't measured yet.

```yaml
  - name:         prediction_noHiC
    params_name:  pred
    lifetime:     75000
    separation:   240
    ctcf_capture: 0.5
    ctcf_type:    my_ctcf_only_sample
```
